title: Fractional Quantum Geometry in Topological Mott Regime
authors: Junyu Tang, Hongquan Lv, Gang v. Chen
abstract: Inspired by recent interests in quantum geometry in electronic bands, we consider a two-dimensional topological Mott insulator, i.e. chiral spin liquid, whose spinon bands develop nontrivial band topological and quantum geometry. The virtual polarization of the gapped charge sector transfers the electromagnetic drive to the charge-neutral spinons through the emergent U(1) gauge field, producing a tensor Ioffe-Larkin response and enabling two complementary optical protocols for measurements. In the off-shell (low-frequency) regime, a self-calibrated ratio of the physical longitudinal and Hall conductivities yields the spinon Chern number without the microscopic knowledge of the charge response. In the on-shell (resonant) regime, combining the inverse Ioffe-Larkin response with the Kramers-Kronig relation enables reconstruction of the quantum-metric and Berry-curvature spectral densities. Our approach directly applies to the triangular lattice Hofstadter-Hubbard model in Moiré systems, can be well adapted to other triangular lattice antiferromagnets such as Nb$_3$Br$_8$ with appropriate modifications. We establish a unified framework for quantitatively probing the quantum geometry of fractionalized quasiparticles in topological Mott regime.
summary: This work develops a theoretical framework to measure the topological properties of fractionalized spinons in a Mott insulator using optical spectroscopy. By analyzing the physical optical response as a combination of charge and spinon effects, the authors propose two protocols: one to extract the quantized spinon Chern number at low frequencies, and another to reconstruct the underlying quantum geometry (metric and Berry curvature) at resonance. This offers a pathway to experimentally verify topological order in strongly correlated quantum magnets.
main_problem: The paper aims to develop quantitative optical protocols to extract the spinon Chern number and reconstruct the hidden quantum geometry of gapped spinon bands in the Topological Mott Regime.
main_result: The low-frequency ratio of longitudinal and Hall conductivities yields a self-calibrated estimator for the spinon Chern number, while an inverse-response Kramers-Kronig protocol allows reconstruction of the quantum metric and Berry curvature spectral densities.
method: The authors use a slave-rotor formulation and analyze the physical optical response as an Ioffe-Larkin composition of charge and spinon responses, applying both low-frequency (off-shell) and resonant (on-shell) measurement techniques.
model_or_system: The study models a two-dimensional topological Mott insulator, specifically using the half-filled triangular-lattice Hofstadter–Hubbard (TLHH) model, which simulates physics in moiré heterostructures under an orbital magnetic flux.
key_observables: Spinon Chern number ($C_s$), physical optical conductivity ($\sigma_{	ext{phys}}(\omega)$), longitudinal ($\sigma_L$) and Hall ($\sigma_H$) conductivities, quantum metric ($g_{ij}$), and Berry curvature ($\Omega_{ij}$).
important_parameters: Orbital flux ($\Phi_\Delta$), spinon gap ($\Delta_s$), and the ratio of hopping to repulsion ($U/t$).
main_assumptions: The analysis relies on the TLHH model as a representative system and assumes that the physical response is an Ioffe-Larkin composition, allowing for the separation of spinon contributions.
figures_summary: Figures illustrate the optical probe mechanism, showing the finite-frequency Chern-number estimator approaching quantized values at low frequency, and comparing direct integration versus reconstruction of the quantum metric and Berry curvature.
paper_structure: The paper first establishes the theoretical framework by deriving the Quantum Geometric Tensor for a two-band model. It then details the measurement protocols: the off-shell limit for the Chern number and the on-shell limit using inverse-response Kramers-Kronig relations to reconstruct spectral densities. Finally, it analyzes the robustness of these measurements against theoretical errors.
why_interesting: The methodology provides a powerful, experimentally relevant framework for probing topological invariants (like the Chern number) in strongly correlated systems using measurable optical responses, which is highly relevant for condensed matter theorists studying correlated materials.
